On the 100-pin TQFP, the debug signals are on port A pins PA00 to PA03, which are package pins 1 to 4. The datasheet's signal tables give pin numbers for the debug signals and for the port names separately. I matched them by pin number, so the PA name for each signal is my inference. The datasheet does not give a combined pin-to-port-to-debug-function line.

- Pin 1, PA00: TDI (JTAG data in).
- Pin 2, PA01: TDO (JTAG data out) and SWO (serial wire output).
- Pin 3, PA02: TMS (JTAG mode select) and SWDIO (SWD data, I/O).
- Pin 4, PA03: TCK (JTAG clock) and SWCLK (SWD clock).

SWD itself only needs SWCLK (PA03) and SWDIO (PA02). SWO (PA01) is optional. Full JTAG uses all four of PA00 to PA03. RESET is a separate dedicated pin, pin 5.

The 100-pin package also has optional instruction-trace pins:
- TRACECLK is pin 11 (PA16).
- TRACE_DATA0 is pin 12 (PA17).
- TRACE_DATA1 is pin 10 (PA15).
- TRACE_DATA2 is pin 9 (PA14).
- TRACE_DATA3 is pin 8 (PA13).

Application note guidance says these should be dedicated to trace when trace is used. It also calls for a 22 Ω series resistor between the trace pins and the trace connector.

**Sharing with other functions:** These pins are normal GPIOs, so they can be shared, but only when no debugger is connected. When a debugger is detected, the JTAG or SWD function is selected on the pad through the PORT mux. That function has higher priority than the GPIO function. User code can't take the pads back by configuring PORT, so the debugger keeps them for as long as it is connected.

- After a power reset, the debug port starts in JTAG mode and claims TCK, TMS, TDI and TDO. If the probe then switches to SWD with the Arm JTAG-to-SWD sequence, only SWCLK and SWDIO are claimed. In that case PA00 and PA01 (TDI and TDO/SWO) are free for other uses.
- Hot-plugging is detected when at least 3 rising edges appear on TCK/SWCLK while RESET is not asserted. This only works while PORT still controls the TCK/SWCLK pad at its reset default. Any change to the PORT configuration of that pad disables hot-plug detection until the next power or external reset. A debugger then can't connect, so don't reconfigure PA03 if you want to attach a debugger later.
- Hot-plugging is also unavailable when DAL.CPU0 is 0 or 3, for security reasons.

For layout, keep the JTAG traces short. If the connector may see ESD, add a series resistor of a few tens of ohms, not more than 100 Ω.

In SERCOM SPI host mode, the pad assignment is set by the CTRLA.DIPO (data in pinout) and CTRLA.DOPO (data out pinout) bit fields.

- DOPO selects the pads for MOSI and SCK (and the host-mode hardware SS output):
  - DOPO=0x0: MOSI on PAD[0], SCK on PAD[1], SS on PAD[2]
  - DOPO=0x1: MOSI on PAD[2], SCK on PAD[3], SS on PAD[1]
  - DOPO=0x2: MOSI on PAD[3], SCK on PAD[1], SS on PAD[2]
  - DOPO=0x3: MOSI on PAD[0], SCK on PAD[3], SS on PAD[1]
- DIPO selects the pad that carries MISO. Any of PAD[0..3] can be chosen with DIPO=0x0 to 0x3. Choose one that doesn't clash with the DOPO pads.

The datasheet's DOPO table lists the exact combinations. Check it for this device, because the PIC32CK table may differ from the older SAM parts. I could not confirm that here.

A common combination is DOPO=0 and DIPO=3: MOSI on PAD0, SCK on PAD1, MISO on PAD3. Another is DOPO=0 and DIPO=2: MISO on PAD2, with SS on PAD2 unavailable for hardware SS use.

Typical wiring for the MCLR/nRESET pin:
- Pull-up: Most PIC32C/SAM devices have an internal pull-up on nRESET (roughly 100 kOhm), so an external pull-up is optional. If you add one, use about 10 kOhm to VDD. Make sure it is not so low that the debugger cannot pull the line low.
- Series resistor: If you add a series resistor between the reset switch/RC network and the pin, keep it small (about 330 Ohm to 1 kOhm). Place it between the pin and any capacitor or switch. Put the debugger connection on the MCU side of the resistor, directly on the pin, so the debugger is not isolated from the pin.
- Capacitor: Keep it small (for example 100 nF at most, and often omitted). A large capacitor slows the edges and can stop the debugger from reliably driving or sensing reset. If you use one, put it on the switch/pull-up side of the series resistor, not on the pin.
- Programmer/debugger: The debugger drives the pin low with an open-drain output. Do not tie the pin directly to VDD, and do not add other drivers or large capacitive loads on the line.

Answering from memory of the LAN8720A datasheet, not from a supplied document, so check the exact figures against the current revision.

The LAN8720A has an internal power-on reset (POR). The datasheet still says an external hardware reset (nRST) is recommended or required in some cases, for these reasons:

1. **Configuration straps.** The PHY latches its strap pins (PHYAD, MODE[2:0], REGOFF, nINTSEL and so on) on the rising edge of POR or nRST. If the supplies or strap levels are not stable when that latch happens, the PHY can come up with the wrong address or mode. A reset applied after the supplies and straps are stable makes it latch the intended configuration.

2. **Supply ramp and the internal regulator.** The internal POR may not be reliable with a slow or non-monotonic VDD ramp, or when the 1.2 V core is supplied externally (REGOFF). An external reset held until the supplies are valid covers this case.

3. **Clock and system sequencing.** The 25 MHz or 50 MHz reference clock must be running and stable before reset is released. A reset also lets the MCU or MAC bring the PHY to a known state, for example after a brown-out or a PHY lock-up. nRST is the only way to do that without power cycling.

4. **Timing.** nRST must be asserted for at least about 100 µs (minimum reset pulse width). After release, wait before MDIO access or traffic. The strap pins need setup and hold time around the nRST rising edge, and the PHY needs a short wait for internal initialization.

In practice, connect nRST to an MCU GPIO or a supervisor/RC circuit. Hold it low through power-up until the supplies and clock are stable, then release it.

I cannot give exact figures from a document here. Check the datasheet's "Reset timing" and "Power-on nRST" sections for the exact minimum pulse width and strap timing.

The PD70100 has an internal N-channel isolation MOSFET (source at VPNIN, drain at VPNOUT) that limits inrush by regulating its current according to the VPNOUT-to-VPNIN voltage. The MOSFET stays high-impedance until VPP-VPNIN reaches the turn-on threshold of 36–42 V. After that it works in one of two modes (Table 1-1):

Limiting the current this way lets a fully discharged bulk capacitor charge at no more than 350 mA, which is compliant with IEEE 802.3af/at. It also avoids a voltage sag at the PD input at power-up. The charge slope is I_inrush / C_DC/DC.

When VPNOUT-VPNIN falls below 0.7 V (max), the switch moves to normal mode and PGOOD is asserted (open-drain, active low).

No documents were provided, so this is general design practice and not taken from a specific datasheet or app note.

Typical placement of the 58 V TVS (for example SMBJ58A, or a similar part such as SMCJ58A for higher surge levels) in a PoE PD front end:

1. **Behind the rectifier, on the DC side.** Place it across the rectified PoE rail (VPORT+ to VPORT−). Put it at the input of the PD interface controller (for example TPS2376 or Si3402), before the hot-swap FET and the DC/DC converter. Keep it close to the PD controller's VDD/VSS pins, with short, wide traces and a solid return to the same ground. This clamps hot-plug inductive spikes and surges that get through the bridge. A 58 V part is chosen because the PoE maximum is 57 V and the standoff voltage is 58 V. Its clamping voltage is about 93 V, so the downstream parts (controller and converter FETs) need to be rated for that.

2. **Ahead of the bulk and hot-swap capacitor.** The TVS goes between the bridge and the PD controller's input capacitor, so it sees the surge first. The 0.1 µF input capacitor, usually 100 V rated, sits next to it.

3. **Optional second TVS on the spare-pair path.** If spare-pair (mode B) power is used, a second TVS goes across that bridge's DC output. Many designs use one TVS after each bridge or after the two bridges are combined.

4. **Lightning surge (Ethernet side).**
   - A 58 V TVS on the DC rail does not protect the data lines or the magnetics.
   - For lightning or IEC 61000-4-5 surges, use a primary protection stage at the RJ45 and magnetics. This can be a Bob Smith termination with a high-voltage (about 1–2 kV) capacitor to chassis ground, plus line-to-line or line-to-ground TVS or low-capacitance diode arrays on the data pairs.

No documents were provided, so this answer comes from general knowledge of IEC 61000-4-5:2005 and not from a cited source. Check the exact figures against the standard or the specific app note.

Waveform and generator
- Shielded or unshielded symmetrical data lines such as Ethernet (10/100/1000BASE-T) are tested with the 1.2/50 µs voltage and 8/20 µs current combination wave. The generator source impedance is 2 Ω.
- For Ethernet lines (symmetrical communication lines), the standard calls for the 10/700 µs generator with a 40 Ω source impedance. That applies to lines that connect to outdoor or long-distance (>300 m) circuits. Product standards such as EN 55035 / EN 55024 often call for the 1.2/50 µs generator with a 42 Ω source impedance (a 40 Ω generator plus 2 Ω) or the 10/700 µs generator.
- Product-standard levels for the Ethernet port are commonly 1 kV line-to-ground, applied through the 10/700 µs generator with the 40 Ω source impedance. Higher levels (2 kV and 4 kV) are used for outdoor or industrial ports.

Test levels in IEC 61000-4-5
- Level 1: 0.5 kV
- Level 2: 1 kV
- Level 3: 2 kV
- Level 4: 4 kV
- "X": open, set by the product specification

Coupling modes
- Ethernet and other symmetrical lines are tested common mode, meaning line(s) to ground. Each pair is coupled to ground through the coupling network. Line-to-line (differential) coupling is not applied to unshielded symmetrical data lines. This is because the coupling transformer and the line-to-line surge are not representative of real-world installations.
- For PoE, the pairs also carry DC power. A coupling/decoupling network (CDN) that does not load the PoE supply must be used, or the PSE and PD are tested as an installed system.
- Polarity is positive and negative, with at least 5 pulses each, at a 1-minute repetition rate or faster. The pulses are applied at 0°, 90° and 270° for AC ports. That phase synchronisation is for AC power ports and is not relevant to the data port.

Unearthed PD
- A PD with no protective earth (floating, double-insulated or battery-style) has no ground reference. The surge must still be applied against a reference ground plane (the coupling is to the ground reference plane, not the PE).
- Because the PD has no earth connection, the surge current has no direct return path to ground. The test is therefore dominated by the insulation withstand between the Ethernet port and the product enclosure/ground plane. Spark-gap or isolation failure across the PoE port transformer is the main concern. That is why the isolation barrier must withstand the full surge voltage. For example, 1.5 kV isolation is typical for Ethernet transformers under IEEE 802.3, and a 2 kV to 6 kV surge may require higher-rated isolation.
- A grounded (earthed) PD is different. The surge current is diverted to PE through the clamping or protection devices (TVS, gas discharge tube, or a Bob Smith termination with a high-voltage capacitor). The test then verifies that the protection works.
- An unearthed PD therefore normally relies on its isolation, and the test is applied from the Ethernet port to the ground reference plane (the product's enclosure or a metal foil wrapped around the product).

- FB1 (pin 8): feedback for the flyback solution. In flyback, it senses the transformer auxiliary winding through a divider R1 (series from winding) / R2 (to GND), sampled during secondary-diode conduction. VREF1 = 1.99 V typ. - FB2 (pin 6): feedback for the non-isolated buck. In a flyback design, connect FB2 to VIN.
- MODE (pin 7): buck/flyback select, pulled up internally to VCC by a 1.5 µA source. In a flyback design, connect MODE directly to GND (float it only for buck). Do not put a resistor between MODE and GND in flyback mode, and do not connect it to VIN in buck mode (p.14).
- ILIM (pin 9): programs the peak switching current limit. Connect a resistor R3 from ILIM to GND (placed close to ILIM/AGND), with ILIM(A) = 100/R3(kΩ) + VL·0.18/L(µH). The limit can't exceed 3 A. For example, R3 = 53.6 kΩ with L = 47 µH gives about 2.05 A typ (p.15, p.4).

The MP6004 has no single fixed switching frequency in flyback mode. It is a variable-frequency DCM/critical-conduction controller, and the frequency depends on peak current, current ramp slew rate and load current.
- Design limit: keep the switching frequency below 200 kHz. The maximum occurs in critical conduction mode at maximum load power.
- Light load: the frequency stretches down automatically at constant IPK. There is an approximate 10 kHz minimum frequency in flyback mode so the output voltage can still be sensed. At very light load, IPK alternates between 20% and 100% of normal IPK. Because of this minimum frequency, a small load is needed to avoid VOUT rising into OVP. In buck mode there is no minimum frequency.
- Upper bound from sensing: the FB sample is taken within 3 µs after the primary MOSFET turns off. The secondary diode conduction time must exceed 3 µs, and this together with the duty cycle sets the maximum frequency.

- Needed to supply the AC ripple current to the inductor/transformer while limiting noise at the input source. It must have low ESR to keep noise at the IC to a minimum.

**EN thresholds (MP6004 electrical characteristics, VIN=48 V, VEN=5 V, TJ −40 to 125 °C):**
- EN high-level voltage: 3.9 V (min). EN is "on" above this.
- EN low-level voltage: 1.3 V (max). EN is "off" below this.
- EN input current: 5.5 µA typ, 7.5 µA max.
- The datasheet gives no typical value for the thresholds. The EN UVLO vs. temperature graph shows the actual rising threshold at about 3.6 V falling to about 2.9 V, and the falling threshold at about 1.9 V falling to about 1.5 V, over −50 to 125 °C (page 6).
- EN is pulled low internally by an approximately 0.9 MΩ resistor. The part turns on when EN goes high and off when EN goes low (page 17).

**EN input limits:**
- Absolute maximum: EN sinking current is 1 mA (note 5). For "all other pins", the voltage range is −0.3 V to +6.5 V. Note 3 says VCC and EN can be pulled above that voltage if the external pull-up current is limited.
- Recommended operating: maximum EN sinking current is 0.5 mA.
- An internal Zener on EN clamps the voltage (assumed 6.5 V). The pull-up current into this clamp must stay below 0.5 mA. Drive EN from a signal below 6.5 V, or through a pull-up resistor that keeps the current below 0.5 mA (page 17).

**Setting a VIN UVLO with EN (page 17, Figure 4):**
- Why: in flyback mode the maximum on-time is about 8 µs. If VIN drops too far, the inductor current cannot reach IPK within that time. The diode conduction time then falls below the 3 µs needed for FB1 sampling, which causes VOUT to drop and then overshoot. EN can shut the part down before this happens.
- The EN thresholds are 3.9 V and 1.3 V, so a plain resistor divider gives a large hysteresis. The datasheet recommends adding a Zener diode (D4) in series with the divider: VIN → D4 → R5 → EN, with R6 from EN to GND.
- Example: turn on before VIN reaches 36 V and shut down before VIN falls to 20 V, using a 20 V Zener with R5 = 100 kΩ and R6 = 49.9 kΩ.
  - Rising threshold: VIN_R < 20 V + (100k + 49.9k)/49.9k × 3.9 V = 31.7 V (Eq. 8).
  - Falling threshold: VIN_F > 20 V + (100k + 49.9k)/49.9k × 1.3 V = 23.9 V (Eq. 9).
- General form, from the equations: VIN_UVLO ≈ VZENER + (R5+R6)/R6 × VEN_threshold, using 3.9 V for rising and 1.3 V for falling.

**EN thresholds (MP6004 Electrical Characteristics, p.4):**
- EN high-level voltage: 3.9 V (the table lists this as a minimum).
- EN low-level voltage: 1.3 V (maximum).
- EN input current: 5.5 µA typical, 7.5 µA maximum. No test condition is given in the table.
- The page-6 typical curve of EN UVLO vs. temperature shows the rising threshold falling from about 3.7 V at -50 °C to about 2.9 V at 150 °C. The falling threshold goes from about 1.9 V to about 1.6 V over the same range. These are read off a graph, so treat them as approximate.

**Operation and input limits (Application Information, p.17):**
- The part turns on when EN goes high and turns off when EN goes low.
- EN is pulled low internally by an approximate 0.9 MΩ resistor.
- An internal Zener on EN clamps the voltage, assumed to be 6.5 V.
- The maximum pull-up current into that clamp must be less than 0.5 mA.
- If you drive EN from an external signal, keep the signal below 6.5 V. Otherwise connect it through a pull-up resistor that limits the current to under 0.5 mA.

**Setting a VIN UVLO with EN:**
- The 3.9 V / 1.3 V thresholds are far apart, so a plain resistor divider from VIN gives a large hysteresis. The datasheet therefore recommends a series Zener diode (D4) plus a divider (R5 from the Zener to EN, R6 from EN to GND), as in Figure 4.
- Rising threshold (Eq. 8): VIN_R ≈ VZ + (R5+R6)/R6 × 3.9 V.
- Falling threshold (Eq. 9): VIN_F ≈ VZ + (R5+R6)/R6 × 1.3 V.
- Worked example: VZ = 20 V, R5 = 100 kΩ, R6 = 49.9 kΩ. This gives a turn-on of about 31.7 V and a turn-off of about 23.9 V. The datasheet's stated goal is on before VIN reaches 36 V and off before it falls to 20 V.
- If VIN − VZENER is above 6.5 V, R5 must satisfy Eq. 10: (VIN − VZENER − 6.5 V)/R5 − 6.5 V/R6 < 0.5 mA.
- Purpose: in flyback mode, a falling VIN can stop the inductor current reaching IPK within the ~8 µs maximum on-time. The diode conduction time then drops below 3 µs, FB1 sampling fails, and VOUT overshoots. The EN-programmed UVLO shuts the part down before this happens.
- The internal VIN UVLO is separate: 11.6 V rising and 8.2 V falling, typical.

Per Microchip's Basic 32-Bit MCU Design and Troubleshooting Checklist (DS70005439B), the USB connector shield should NOT be directly connected to the digital logic ground (Table 11-5, rule 6). Differential signals have good noise immunity, but they are still susceptible to ground loops that create offsets on the signal level thresholds. A capacitor between the USB shield and logic ground is also not good practice, because it conducts an ESD discharge directly into the MCU system.

Section 11.6.1 (Key USB Host Design Points, Figure 11-10) says that tying the shield to digital ground is a typical design error. It lets an ESD discharge event get into the digital ground system, which can reset the MCU or damage components. Instead:
- Attach the shield to chassis (AC) ground. This is the preferred option, if the chassis ground is accessible.
- If chassis ground is not accessible, connect the shield to digital ground through one of two parts:
  - Recommended: a 10 kΩ fixed resistor. It gives ESD protection and also isolates ground-loop current between the remote system's shield or case and the local digital ground. 10 kΩ is low enough impedance that RF and EMI are still attenuated, so the cable shield stays effective.
  - A ferrite bead rated 1 kΩ @ 100 MHz, 1 A, DCR 0.15 Ω (for example MI0805J102R-10). Use this only where ESD protection is the concern.
- In the Figure 11-10 example, connector pin 4 (GND) goes to digital ground through a BLM31KN471SN1L ferrite bead (480 Ω @ 100 MHz, 4 A). There is no series resistor on this connection, because of the potentially large USB downstream power requirements.

TLA2518 is an 8-channel, 12-bit SAR ADC with SPI. It is the lower-speed sibling of the ADS7138-class parts.

- When acquisition happens: the device uses CS-controlled timing. On the CS falling edge the ADC samples the input and ends acquisition, so the input is held at that point. Conversion starts then. Conversion runs after CS falls and finishes before the next acquisition. Acquisition is the interval from the end of conversion to the next CS falling edge. Conversion data is shifted out on the following frame, so the output lags the sample by one cycle.

Treat the acquisition and conversion timing numbers as not stated here. Look them up in the datasheet's timing requirements table and its cycle-timing figure.

When acquisition happens: conversion starts on the rising edge of CS, and the ADC converts sample N for t_CONV. After the conversion finishes, the ADC acquires sample N+1 for the rest of the cycle (t_ACQ), until the next CS rising edge. The data for the previous sample is read out over SPI during this acquisition window. Data from sample N is clocked out on SDO during this acquisition phase. So tCYCLE = tCONV + tACQ, which at 1 MSPS is 600 ns max + 400 ns min = 1 µs.
